item.text: The evidence now shows a mixed 2022 trajectory rather than a simple “recovery” story: insurance coverage and mortality improved, federal relief and infrastructure programs reached vulnerable groups, and durable health/water legislation was enacted; at the same time child poverty and food insecurity rose sharply after temporary relief expired, health affordability remained poor, learning losses were severe and unequal, and audits found important oversight/data weaknesses. item.text:
## 1. Orientation

**Scope:** Joe Biden, United States, calendar year 2022 only. No chapter score is assigned. `score_1_to_10: null` because scoring was expressly excluded, not because evidence is insufficient.

**Authority.** Biden controlled the federal executive branch and supervised implementation of federal law, but Congress controlled appropriations and most durable expansions of social benefits. States, territories, tribes, school districts, health systems, and local grantees delivered much of Medicaid, education, housing, water, and public-health policy. Consequently, enactments such as the Inflation Reduction Act and Bipartisan Infrastructure Law receive shared presidential–congressional attribution; implementation by Treasury, CMS, EPA, CDC, and Education receives stronger executive attribution; national outcomes receive only limited or shared attribution. These boundaries follow the Constitution’s Take Care, Spending, and Appropriations clauses. [Constitution Annotated](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artII-S3-3-1/ALDE_00001160), [National Archives](https://www.archives.gov/founding-docs/constitution-transcript).

**Inherited baseline and shocks.** Biden inherited a wealthy, very-high-human-development country but with pronounced racial, income, geographic, health-access, housing, and educational inequalities. The immediate baseline also included accumulated COVID-19 mortality, school disruption, supply-chain problems, and previously enacted emergency programs. During 2022, Omicron and later variants continued; Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, food and energy shocks, and domestic supply constraints contributed to inflation. December 2022 prices were 6.5% above December 2021, with food prices up 10.4%. [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_01122023.htm).

**Central balance.** Material favorable evidence includes record ACA Marketplace enrollment and lower premiums; a lower uninsured rate; distribution of free COVID tests; falling COVID and all-cause mortality; targeted vaccine, rental, education, and water programs; and enactment of durable ACA-subsidy and Medicare-drug reforms. Material adverse evidence includes expiration of the expanded Child Tax Credit and stimulus support, followed by a reported doubling of child supplemental poverty; increased food insecurity; severe and unequal learning losses; persistent health-cost barriers and racial mortality disparities; low young-child vaccination; and substantial shortcomings in relief oversight and public-health measurement.

The poverty comparison needs special caution: in July 2026 BLS disclosed coding errors in the 2019–2024 Supplemental Poverty Measure thresholds. Census says revised poverty rates have not yet been released. The published direction and policy explanation remain evidence, but exact magnitudes are now provisional. [Census Bureau correction notice and original analysis](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2023/09/supplemental-poverty-measure.html).

**Information environment.** The United States had open statistics, audits, courts, congressional oversight, press, and civil-society criticism. Data quality is generally high, but federalism weakens attribution; administrative systems have missing recipient and race data; point-in-time homelessness counts have known coverage limits; and some 2022 outcomes reflect earlier policy or pandemic dynamics. The workspace’s local guide and registry could not be directly opened through the available research interface, so the supplied registry principles were followed and this limitation is recorded.

**Structured prior summary:** UNDP’s 2021/22 report supplies a high-level pandemic human-development prior, not a Biden-performance finding. WDI and V-Dem leads did not supply sufficiently precise, target-year ruler-attributable facts for acceptance. National Census, CDC, USDA, NCES, CMS, EPA, GAO, and independent survey evidence therefore carries the dossier.

## 2. Compact evidence index

## 3. Ten-question disposition

1. **6B.1 — Welfare as a core purpose:** Well evidenced but mixed. ACA affordability, testing, rental, school-recovery, water, and durable Medicare reforms show substantive activity beyond rhetoric (WEB-6B-002, 010–014). Expiration of major family relief and worsening material hardship weigh against an unqualified finding (WEB-6B-004–005).

2. **6B.2 — Basic-service access:** Strongly evidenced for health, education, water, housing, food, and social protection. Insurance and Marketplace access improved; water and education funds were delivered. Affordability, food security, learning, and housing administration remained serious weaknesses (WEB-6B-002–013, 018). Sanitation apart from water infrastructure is weakly evidenced.

3. **6B.3 — Vulnerable groups:** Strong evidence of explicit prioritization—low-income renters, disadvantaged water systems, marginalized vaccine groups, underrepresented students, older Medicare beneficiaries, and disabled test users. Significant racial, rural, maternal, educational, and vaccination disparities remained (WEB-6B-008–012, 014, 016, 018).

4. **6B.4 — Professional administration:** Evidence supports normal agency/professional administration rather than patronage, especially through CMS, EPA, CDC, Education, Treasury, and statistical agencies. GAO nevertheless found incomplete data, weak risk assessment, and insufficient strategic measurement (WEB-6B-010–012, 016–017). This dossier found no demonstrated welfare patronage network.

5. **6B.5 — Evidence and correction:** Substantial measurement existed through Census, CDC/NCHS, USDA, NCES, program dashboards, and GAO. Districts reported using data; OMB implemented a GAO payment-data certification recommendation in September 2022. Conversely, CDC strategies initially lacked objectives and performance measures, ERA data were incomplete, and the later Census threshold error reduces confidence (WEB-6B-004, 010–012, 017).

6. **6B.6 — Crisis suffering:** Free tests, vaccines, treatments, education aid, rental aid, and continuing insurance protection reduced some suffering; mortality declined sharply. Approximately 245,000 COVID-associated deaths still occurred in 2022, with marked group and regional differences, while food insecurity and child poverty rose as support receded (WEB-6B-004–005, 010–018).

7. **6B.7 — Political loyalty or punishment:** No accepted source established that Biden conditioned ordinary welfare benefits on personal or partisan loyalty. Statutory income, age, need, or program-compliance conditions are not evidence of political punishment. This is a moderately searched absence, not proof that no local incident occurred.

8. **6B.8 — Dignity and equal opportunity:** Disability-accessible tests, translation, community clinics, disadvantaged-community water funding, and protections for underserved students support favorable intent and some implementation. Persistent Black maternal mortality, unequal learning loss, rural child-vaccine gaps, and cost-related care avoidance show that equal opportunity was far from achieved (WEB-6B-006, 008–012, 014, 016, 018).

9. **6B.9 — Durability:** The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act’s ACA and Medicare provisions and the five-year water-infrastructure appropriations were durable institutional changes. ESSER and emergency rental funds were temporary, the expanded CTC expired, and many IRA beneficiary effects began only after 2022 (WEB-6B-004, 010–013, 017).

10. **6B.10 — Overall life chances:** Mixed trajectory. Insurance coverage, life expectancy, maternal mortality, COVID mortality, and future institutional capacity improved. Real income fell, child poverty and food insecurity increased, learning losses were severe, infant mortality rose, and health affordability remained weak. Causal attribution is strongest for enacted and administered programs, weaker for national outcomes (WEB-6B-002–018).

**Evidenced domains:** health, education, drinking water/wastewater infrastructure, housing/rental assistance, food security, and social protection.  
**Weak domains:** sanitation outcomes distinct from infrastructure funding, disability services beyond selected programs, childcare quality, long-term housing production, and welfare conditionality at subnational level.

## 4. Source dispositions

**Independent corroboration**

- Census CPS/ACS corroborates CMS enrollment direction, though definitions differ.
- CDC/NCHS final mortality data corroborate the earlier provisional COVID-mortality report.
- GAO independently tests agency claims concerning vaccine equity, ERA, education spending, and public-health management.
- Commonwealth Fund independently shows that coverage gains did not eliminate affordability barriers.
- NAEP independently tests whether education-recovery spending had yet translated into national learning recovery.
- BLS inflation data corroborate the cost shock underlying income, food, and affordability pressures.

**Reused supplied records**

- E014 reopened and accepted as WEB-6B-016.
- E015 reopened but treated as corroboration rather than an atomic accepted record because its composite adult-vaccination measure spans several vaccines and has weak Biden attribution.
- E016 reopened and accepted as WEB-6B-018.
- E017 reopened and accepted as WEB-6B-006.
- E018 remained corroborative implementation context; it added no material fact beyond the stronger GAO vaccine record.

**Uninspected leads**

- V-Dem equality country-year observations.
- WDI education and inequality series.
- Full HUD 2022 AHAR PDF and underlying PIT tables.
- Detailed state-by-state Medicaid continuous-coverage records.
- ILO/UNESCO/WHO cross-country tables where U.S. target-year values were not extractable from the opened pages.

**Rejected**

- White House promotional summaries where CMS, EPA, statute, or GAO provided a stronger underlying record.
- Later partisan Education Department characterizations of Biden student-loan policy.
- Later implementation achievements used as if they were 2022 outcomes.
- Generic UNDP global decline statements as evidence of Biden performance.
- Search snippets or PDF index text lacking an inspected supporting passage.

**Blocked**

- One direct Congress.gov fetch was blocked by robots controls. Accessible Constitution Annotated, statutory summaries, CMS, and CBO pages supplied the needed underlying facts.

## 5. Discovery counts

Operational counts after deduplication:

- Distinct source leads reviewed: **43**
- Fully accepted atomic records: **18**
- Accepted records that reuse supplied leads: **4**
- Independent corroboration sources retained: **6**
- Partial/landing-page sources: **2**
- Uninspected leads: **5**
- Rejected or superseded leads: **7**
- Blocked source attempts: **1**

Counts describe source disposition, not independent-event weight.

## 6. Remaining research questions

Further research could materially improve:

- state-level Medicaid, housing, school-recovery, and rural/tribal implementation;
- final revised 2019–2024 SPM estimates after the 2026 threshold correction;
- sanitation outcomes and actual lead-line replacements completed during 2022;
- distribution of relief by disability, tribal status, immigration status, and U.S. territory;
- rigorous causal evaluations separating ARPA effects from labor-market recovery and state policy;
- systematic searches of grant or benefit retaliation complaints.

Additional broad national searching is unlikely to change the central mixed balance; targeted subnational and causal-evaluation work could.

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2022","publisher":"CDC National Center for Health Statistics","publication_date":"2024-05","url":"https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/hestat/maternal-mortality/2022/maternal-mortality-rates-2022.htm","claim":"Maternal mortality fell from 32.9 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2021 to 22.3 in 2022, but the Black maternal mortality rate remained 49.5, significantly above White, Hispanic, and Asian rates.","locator":"Opening five paragraphs; Figures 1-3 and table","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"maternal_mortality_inequality_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Adds a gender- and race-specific dignity and equal-opportunity outcome with both improvement and severe residual disparity.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"final outcome statistic","period_fit":"later final statistical evidence for 2022","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["maternal_health","racial_equity","mortality"],"source_type":"national vital statistics","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Official final mortality and natality files, with acknowledged pregnancy-checkbox and small-number limitations.","final_evidence_use":"Mixed maternal-health and distribution evidence.","ruler_attribution":"limited because pandemic intensity, state maternity systems, insurance, clinical care, and demographic factors jointly determine the outcome","contrary_evidence":"Year-to-year rates fluctuate, and reporting accuracy limits causal interpretation; the racial gap remained extremely large.","source_dependencies":["NVSS mortality and natality files"],"lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.8","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"NAEP Long-Term Trend Assessment Results: Reading and Mathematics","publisher":"National Center for Education Statistics","publication_date":"2022-09","url":"https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/highlights/ltt/2022/","claim":"Among nine-year-olds, reading scores fell five points and mathematics seven points from 2020 to 2022; lower-performing students declined more, and the White-Black mathematics gap widened from 25 to 33 points.","locator":"Overview; Recent Student Performance Trends; Performance Trends by Student Group","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"naep_learning_loss_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Provides direct nationally standardized evidence of severe and unequal educational loss at the inherited-to-2022 boundary.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"education outcome statistic","period_fit":"contemporaneous 2022 assessment comparing with pre-disruption 2020","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["education_quality","distribution","pandemic_baseline"],"source_type":"national standardized assessment","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"NCES national assessment using established scales and significance testing.","final_evidence_use":"Decisive adverse education and equal-opportunity evidence.","ruler_attribution":"limited: most disruption predated Biden and schooling is state/local, though federal recovery leadership and funding were within his shared authority","contrary_evidence":"The comparison captures cumulative pandemic disruption, not solely 2022 policy, and some location gaps narrowed.","source_dependencies":["NAEP long-term trend sampling and assessment"],"lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.8","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"K-12 Education: School Districts Reported Spending Initial COVID Relief Funds on Meeting Students' Needs and Continuing School Operations","publisher":"U.S. Government Accountability Office","publication_date":"2024-09-23","url":"https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-106913","claim":"By the end of school year 2021-22 districts had spent nearly $60 billion in ESSER funds; about 80 percent addressed academic, social and emotional needs or school operations, while the remainder addressed physical and mental health, and 16 of 17 visited districts used data to examine activities.","locator":"Fast Facts and What GAO Found, paragraphs 1-4","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"esser_delivery_school_year_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Confirms actual education-relief delivery, service uses, and local evidence practices rather than relying on federal appropriations alone.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"later implementation evaluation","period_fit":"later retrospective using school-year 2021-22 expenditure data","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["education_delivery","professional_administration","evaluation"],"source_type":"independent federal performance audit","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"GAO analysis of Education data plus purposive visits; national spending results are strong, district qualitative findings are illustrative.","final_evidence_use":"Favorable delivery and measurement evidence, limited by uncertain effect and durability.","ruler_attribution":"shared/institutional because funding came from multiple laws and Congress, while Education oversight and ARPA implementation occurred under Biden and districts selected uses","contrary_evidence":"GAO could not isolate individual activity effects, insufficient time had passed to assess durability, and the funds were temporary.","source_dependencies":["Education Department ESSER data","17 selected district visits"],"lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.9"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"Emergency Rental Assistance: Treasury's Oversight Is Limited by Incomplete Data and Risk Assessment","publisher":"U.S. Government Accountability Office","publication_date":"2022-12-20","url":"https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-23-105410","claim":"Limited data indicated 85 percent of ERA1 households served had incomes below 50 percent of area median, but Treasury's $3.1 billion reallocation through October 2022 did not consistently align funds with interstate renter need, and recipient/payment data and improper-payment risk assessment were incomplete.","locator":"What GAO Found, lines 276-294","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"era_targeting_and_oversight_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Combines demonstrated low-income targeting with precise administrative, allocation, and measurement weaknesses in a major housing-protection program.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"implementation audit and procedural finding","period_fit":"contemporaneous through October 2022","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["housing","low_income_targeting","audit","federalism"],"source_type":"independent federal performance audit","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"GAO analyzed program and demographic data and interviewed 21 grantees; it explicitly notes incomplete data.","final_evidence_use":"Mixed housing-access, vulnerable-group, competence, and evidence-use finding.","ruler_attribution":"authority-based/shared: Treasury administration was under Biden; Congress created the programs and nonfederal grantees delivered aid","contrary_evidence":"Third-party studies and eviction data suggested ERA limited evictions, and local flexibility served differing needs; incomplete data prevent full outcome measurement.","source_dependencies":["Treasury grantee reporting","21 selected grantee interviews"],"lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8","6B.9"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"EPA Celebrates Year One Accomplishments Under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law","publisher":"U.S. Environmental Protection Agency","publication_date":"2022-11","url":"https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-celebrates-year-one-accomplishments-under-bipartisan-infrastructure-law","claim":"EPA reported awarding $5.5 billion of $14.1 billion available in FY2022, including 20 state capitalization grants for lead-line identification and replacement expected to fund about 300 projects, with nearly half of relevant revolving-fund resources directed to disadvantaged communities.","locator":"Year One accomplishments bullets and FY2022 funding section","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"bil_water_delivery_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Moves water policy evidence from authorization to 2022 awards and shows statutory/discretionary equity design.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"implementation and administrative output","period_fit":"contemporaneous FY2022 implementation","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["water","infrastructure","environmental_justice","durability"],"source_type":"executing-agency administrative report","source_confidence":"medium-high","source_confidence_reason":"Official award information is strong for obligations and program design but is not an independent measure of completed pipes or health outcomes.","final_evidence_use":"Favorable water-access, equity, and durable-capacity evidence.","ruler_attribution":"shared: bipartisan congressional enactment signed by Biden; EPA allocation guidance and implementation were executive actions","contrary_evidence":"Awards and expected projects are not completed infrastructure or demonstrated 2022 water-quality gains; states choose projects.","source_dependencies":["Bipartisan Infrastructure Law appropriations","state revolving funds"],"lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.8","6B.9"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"Anniversary of the Inflation Reduction Act: Update on CMS Implementation","publisher":"Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services","publication_date":"2023-08-16","url":"https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/anniversary-inflation-reduction-act-update-cms-implementation","claim":"The Inflation Reduction Act, signed August 16, 2022, extended enhanced Marketplace subsidies through 2025 and created durable Medicare drug-cost reforms, but major beneficiary provisions such as the $35 covered-insulin cap and zero-cost recommended adult vaccines began January 1, 2023.","locator":"Opening paragraphs and provision bullets","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"ira_health_institutions_enacted_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Documents a durable 2022 institutional change while preventing post-2022 beneficiary effects from being misclassified as target-year outcomes.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"policy enactment and implementation timeline","period_fit":"immediate retrospective on 2022 enactment; later effects explicitly separated","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["health_affordability","elderly","durability","period_boundary"],"source_type":"federal administrative legal summary","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"CMS is the implementing authority and gives statutory dates; CBO independently supports the drug-pricing mechanism.","final_evidence_use":"Favorable revealed priority and durability evidence, not counted as a 2022 drug-cost outcome.","ruler_attribution":"shared/direct advocacy: Congress enacted the law, Biden negotiated for and signed it, and his administration implemented it","contrary_evidence":"Most direct Medicare savings began after 2022; Marketplace subsidy extension preserved rather than newly expanded 2022 access.","source_dependencies":["Public Law 117-169","CMS implementation"],"lenses":["6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"ASPR Testimony on the Federal COVID-19 Response","publisher":"U.S. Department of Health and Human Services","publication_date":"2023-02-08","url":"https://www.hhs.gov/about/agencies/asl/testimony/2023/02/08/federal-response-covid-19.html","claim":"After Biden announced one billion free at-home tests in January 2022, HHS and the Postal Service delivered more than 720 million tests, including an accessible test for blind and low-vision users.","locator":"ASPR testimony, testing section, paragraphs beginning 'ASPR continues to support access'","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"free_covid_tests_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Provides a concrete, high-volume crisis service with a disability-access feature directly implemented under Biden.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"implementation output","period_fit":"immediate retrospective of program begun in 2022","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["pandemic_response","testing","disability_access"],"source_type":"executive-agency testimony","source_confidence":"medium-high","source_confidence_reason":"Official operational count given in congressional testimony; independent performance or uptake evaluation is not supplied.","final_evidence_use":"Favorable crisis mitigation, access, and dignity evidence.","ruler_attribution":"direct presidential initiative and executive implementation, with Postal Service partnership and congressional funding constraints","contrary_evidence":"Tests alone do not establish timely use, equitable household distribution, or reduced mortality, and internet/mail access could exclude some people.","source_dependencies":["ASPR procurement records","Postal Service distribution"],"lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.6","6B.8"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"COVID-19 Mortality Update — United States, 2022","publisher":"CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report","publication_date":"2023-05-05","url":"https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7218a4.htm","claim":"COVID-19 was associated with approximately 244,986 deaths in 2022, while the age-adjusted rate fell 47 percent from 2021; rates remained highest among adults 85 and older and American Indian or Alaska Native people and varied substantially across HHS regions.","locator":"Summary; Results; Table 1; Discussion","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"covid_mortality_distribution_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Quantifies both the continuing crisis burden and the unequal distribution behind the aggregate mortality improvement.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"provisional outcome statistic","period_fit":"immediate retrospective for 2022","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["pandemic_mortality","distribution","regional_variation"],"source_type":"national mortality surveillance","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"More than 99 percent of 2022 death records had been received; later final NCHS data corroborate the broad decline, with small count differences from provisional coding.","final_evidence_use":"Mixed crisis-outcome evidence with strong distribution caveats.","ruler_attribution":"limited/shared because variants, vaccines developed earlier, prior immunity, treatment, behavior, states, and federal policy all contributed","contrary_evidence":"The decline cannot be assigned wholly to administration action; approximately 245,000 associated deaths remained and child rates increased.","source_dependencies":["NVSS death certificates","Census population estimates"],"lenses":["6B.3","6B.6","6B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"COVID-19: Federal Efforts to Provide Vaccines to Racial and Ethnic Groups","publisher":"U.S. Government Accountability Office","publication_date":"2021-12-10","url":"https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105079","claim":"CDC, HRSA, and FEMA used race and ethnicity data, translation, extended hours, outreach and pop-up clinics to serve underserved groups; CDC exceeded its 40 percent retail-program target, but Black people remained underrepresented relative to population and race data were incomplete.","locator":"Fast Facts and What GAO Found, lines 264-292","provisional_id":"E014","canonical_fact_key":"federal_vaccine_equity_programs","new_fact_contribution":"Independently verifies concrete equity-oriented delivery mechanisms and residual disparity rather than accepting agency intent alone.","inspection_state":"reused_opened_source","evidence_status":"implementation audit and distribution comparison","period_fit":"inherited and continuing program context entering 2022","disposition":"accepted as inherited/contextual implementation evidence","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["vaccine_equity","vulnerable_groups","audit"],"source_type":"independent federal performance audit","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"GAO reviewed three programs and directly cautioned about missing race and ethnicity data.","final_evidence_use":"Favorable targeting evidence with material adverse distribution limitation.","ruler_attribution":"shared/institutional because programs began under Biden in February 2021 and continued into 2022, while states and private pharmacies delivered doses","contrary_evidence":"Black representation remained below population share; missing demographic data might explain some or all observed differences.","source_dependencies":["CDC, HRSA and FEMA program data"],"lenses":["6B.3","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.8"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"COVID-19: Current and Future Federal Preparedness Requires Fixes to Improve Health Data and Address Improper Payments","publisher":"U.S. Government Accountability Office","publication_date":"2022-04-27","url":"https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105397","claim":"By March 2022 agencies had fully or partly addressed only 39 percent of GAO's 279 pandemic recommendations; GAO found CDC surveillance lacked specific objectives and progress measures and data-modernization plans lacked actions and timelines, while OMB implemented GAO's payment-data certification recommendation in September 2022.","locator":"Fast Facts and What GAO Found, lines 264-316; recommendation status lines 352-359","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"covid_management_measurement_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Supplies both a contemporaneous professional-management deficiency and a documented 2022 corrective action.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"final audit finding and procedural correction","period_fit":"contemporaneous 2022 audit; September 2022 correction recorded in recommendation status","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["professional_administration","measurement","correction","pandemic_preparedness"],"source_type":"independent federal performance audit","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"GAO reviewed federal documents, data, and interviews and tracked agency responses.","final_evidence_use":"Mixed evidence on competence, evidence use, transparent correction, and crisis durability.","ruler_attribution":"authority-based: deficiencies and OMB correction occurred in executive agencies supervised by Biden, though many systems and recommendations were inherited","contrary_evidence":"The recommendation denominator accumulated from June 2020 and therefore includes pre-Biden failures; agencies had made progress and later completed further corrections.","source_dependencies":["GAO cumulative COVID oversight portfolio","agency submissions"],"lenses":["6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.9"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"COVID-19 Vaccination Coverage and Demographic Characteristics of Infants and Children Aged 6 Months–4 Years — United States, June 20–December 31, 2022","publisher":"CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report","publication_date":"2023-02-17","url":"https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7207a4.htm","claim":"By December 31, 2022 only 10.1 percent of U.S. children aged six months through four years had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose, with coverage 10.5 percent in urban areas versus 3.4 percent in rural areas and wide state variation.","locator":"Table, United States row, lines 157-174; Summary and Discussion","provisional_id":"E016","canonical_fact_key":"young_child_covid_vaccine_inequality_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Adds target-period uptake evidence showing that availability and equity initiatives did not produce broad or geographically equal protection for young children.","inspection_state":"reused_opened_source","evidence_status":"implementation uptake outcome","period_fit":"covers June 20 through December 31, 2022","disposition":"accepted","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["child_health","vaccination","rural_inequality"],"source_type":"national administrative surveillance study","source_confidence":"medium-high","source_confidence_reason":"CDC jurisdictional administration data provide direct counts, but denominators and reporting varied and some jurisdictions had incomplete demographic data.","final_evidence_use":"Adverse child-access and distribution evidence.","ruler_attribution":"shared/limited because federal approval, procurement and messaging interacted with pediatricians, parents, states, and local access","contrary_evidence":"Eligibility began only in June 2022, so the uptake window was short; hesitancy and local delivery were not solely under federal control.","source_dependencies":["state and jurisdiction immunization systems","Census denominators"],"lenses":["6B.2","6B.3","6B.6","6B.8"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"Consumer Price Index — December 2022","publisher":"U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics","publication_date":"2023-01-12","url":"https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_01122023.htm","claim":"The CPI-U was 6.5 percent higher in December 2022 than a year earlier, while the food index was 10.4 percent higher, documenting a major cost-of-living shock affecting real household welfare.","locator":"Opening release paragraphs and 12-month changes section","provisional_id":null,"canonical_fact_key":"us_inflation_food_price_shock_2022","new_fact_contribution":"Provides an external constraint and mechanism relevant to falling real income, food insecurity, and affordability without treating the shock as wholly presidential.","inspection_state":"opened_underlying_source","evidence_status":"economic context statistic","period_fit":"contemporaneous calendar-year-end 2022","disposition":"accepted as contextual constraint","chapter_ids":["6B"],"methodology_ids":["inflation","food_prices","external_shock"],"source_type":"official price statistics","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Standard national CPI methodology from the independent federal statistical agency.","final_evidence_use":"Constraint and adverse household-affordability context, not a standalone welfare-performance finding.","ruler_attribution":"limited and disputed: fiscal, monetary, supply-chain, energy, war, demand, and corporate pricing factors all contributed","contrary_evidence":"Inflation slowed late in 2022, employment conditions improved, and CPI does not measure household resources or distribution directly.","source_dependencies":["BLS consumer price sample"],"lenses":["6B.2","6B.6","6B.10"]}

items.text: Inspect local research guide, registry, and available priors
Establish authority, baseline, shocks, and information environment
Research favorable, adverse, disputed, and exculpatory evidence across all ten lenses
Validate evidence records, citations, locators, attribution, and JSON
Deliver compact dossier, gaps, counts, and machine records without a score
